title: The Endurance Runner, the Hearth & Salivary Starch — 1.53-Ma KNM-WT 15000 Turkana Boy Endurance Running & Eccrine Sweating (Bramble & Lieberman), 1.8-Ma Dmanisi Skull 5, 1.0-Ma Wonderwerk Cave FTIR Hearth, Wrangham's Cooking Hypothesis, Human AMY1 & Dog AMY2B Starch Copy-Number Expansion (PDB 1SMD, 1MFU, 1XV8)

teenKit.tldr: Humans evolved an energy-hogging brain and endurance-running body while somehow running on less overall fuel than expected, solving a massive biological paradox. This incredible upgrade relied on sweat glands, cooking food, and extra gene copies to digest starch.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our ancestors hacked their metabolism reveals the evolutionary secrets behind why modern humans can process carbs so efficiently and run long distances without overheating.
keyTakeaways: The Expensive Tissue Paradox highlights how humans defied basic physics by fueling a massive, energy-hungry brain without drastically increasing total food intake.
Breezy cooling systems—like our unique eccrine sweat glands and narrow waistlines—turned early humans into elite long-distance endurance runners.
Cooking food and multiplying our starch-digestion genes (AMY1) unlocked a dense, easy-to-absorb calorie source that fed our growing brains.

vocab.meaning: The evolutionary puzzle of how humans grew a massive, calorie-hungry brain while shrinking our digestive tract and overall energy input.
The human superpower of sweating watery fluid all over the skin to cool down efficiently during intense, long-distance movement.
The idea that discovering fire and cooking food chemically pre-digested meals, giving humans way more calories with less chewing and digestive effort.
The genetic code for salivary amylase, an enzyme in our spit that breaks down starches, which humans have multiplied to digest carbs better.

quiz.question: What is the 'Expensive Tissue Paradox' in human evolution?
options: How humans got taller without growing heavier bones
How humans fueled a giant, energy-demanding brain without a massive increase in total daily calories
Why human babies require more expensive care than other primates
How our muscles became weaker to make room for bigger organs
quiz.explanation: It describes the puzzle of how our energy-hogging brain evolved while our overall metabolic budget stayed surprisingly flat.

quiz.question: Which adaptation was crucial for early humans to become long-distance endurance runners without overheating?
options: Thick fur coats to block the sun
Widespread eccrine sweat glands across the body
A shorter stride length to conserve energy
quiz.explanation: Eccrine sweating allows humans to evaporate heat efficiently across their entire skin surface, preventing heat exhaustion during long chases.

quiz.question: How did duplicating the AMY1 gene help human ancestors?
options: It allowed them to run faster sprints in short bursts
It gave them better night vision in dark caves
It increased their sweat production in hot climates
It produced more salivary enzymes to break down starchy foods and extract extra calories
quiz.explanation: Extra copies of the AMY1 gene meant more starch-digesting enzymes in saliva, helping early humans squeeze maximum energy out of cooked tubers and carbs.
